pll1d3c3-d1e3476.summary: Warns with Augustine that the image made by the Trinity must not be thought wholly like it: in whatever likeness there is great unlikeness.
claims: The image is not wholly similar to the Trinity.
Great unlikeness accompanies the likeness.

pll1d3c3-qboiee.summary: First dissimilarity: one man remembers, understands, and loves through the three but is not them, while in God's simplicity the three persons are the one God. The Trinity is one thing, its image in another thing is another, and man is called image because of what is in him, as a panel is called a picture.
claims: A human being has memory, understanding, and love but is not them.
In God the three persons are the one God.
Man is called image because of the trinity in him, as a panel is called an image because of its painting.

pll1d3c3-d1e3506.summary: Second dissimilarity: the human image is one person, while the Trinity is three persons. In man the three belong to the one person; in God they are not 'of' God but are God, and are three persons. It asks whether the Trinity could be in God as something of God that is not God.
claims: The human image is one person; the Trinity is three persons.
In man the three belong to a man; in God the three are God.

pll1d3c3-d1e3530.summary: Rejects the idea of a Trinity that is not God and concludes that the mind's image is slight and mostly unlike. Adds that the mind is God's image not only because it knows and loves itself but because it can remember, understand, and love its maker.
claims: The Trinity is not something of God that is not God.
The image in the mind is small and largely dissimilar.
The mind is God's image chiefly because it can remember, know, and love God.

pll1d3c3-d1e3555.summary: Introduces another way, with other names, of distinguishing a trinity in the soul as image of the Trinity.

pll1d3c3-d1e3559.summary: Gives the triad mind, its knowledge, and its love from De Trinitate IX: the mind knows and loves itself and cannot love itself without knowing itself. The three are distinct yet one because they exist substantially in the soul; 'mind' here means its most excellent part.
claims: Mind, knowledge, and love are three.
The mind cannot love itself unless it knows itself.
They are one because they exist substantially in the soul.

pll1d3c3-d1e3593.summary: Develops the triad's Trinitarian structure: the mind is parent, generating its self-knowledge as offspring; love proceeds from both as the embrace of parent and offspring. Each is equal to the others when the mind knows and loves itself as much as it is, and each is in the others.
claims: The mind begets its knowledge as parent begets offspring.
Love proceeds from mind and knowledge.
Offspring and love are not less than the parent.
Each of the three is in the others.

pll1d3c3-d1e3608.summary: Concludes that in these three some vestige of the Trinity appears.
claims: Mind, knowledge, and love show a trace of the Trinity.

pll1d3c3-d1e3611.summary: Describes the ascent: considering these three in one essence, the rational mind contemplates the Creator and sees unity in trinity. It reasons there is one God, since two would be either insufficient or one superfluous; that God is not without wisdom, which is begotten of him; and that he loves his wisdom, so love is there too.
claims: There is one God, one essence, one principle.
Two gods would be either insufficient or redundant.
God has a wisdom begotten from him.
Because God loves his wisdom, there is love in God.

pl-l1d3c3.summary: Stresses the great unlikeness within the likeness of the mental image. In man one person has memory, understanding, and love but is not them, whereas God is the three persons; the image belongs to one person while the Trinity is three persons. The mind is God's image chiefly because it can remember, understand, and love its maker. A second Augustinian triad, mind, knowledge, and love, is laid out as parent, offspring, and the love that proceeds from both, mutually equal and mutually indwelling. From considering this, the rational mind rises to see unity in trinity: there must be one God (two would be either insufficient or redundant), who has a begotten wisdom and loves it.
claims: The likeness of the image to the Trinity includes great unlikeness.
A man has memory, understanding, and love but is not them; God is the three persons.
The human image is one person; the Trinity is three persons.
The mind is God's image chiefly because it can remember, understand, and love God.
Mind, knowledge, and love form a trinity of parent, offspring, and proceeding love, equal and mutually indwelling.
There can be only one God, since two would be either insufficient or redundant.
Reason can see that God has wisdom begotten from him and love for it.
